_podcast.theme_scoring_prompt:
Rate how well this article fits the theme 'Arts, Culture & Digital Storytelling' — how communities create, preserve, and share culture, with particular interest in the Cariboo and rural BC.

OUT OF SCOPE — score 0-14: medical and health research with no cultural angle; resource-economy stories with no cultural framing; wildlife and nature stories without a creative or community-media context; data centre and AI investment news; geopolitical conflict, war, and crime coverage; financial market stories.

CALIBRATION — apply this ladder to everything else. A Cariboo tie raises a score but is NOT required to reach the top band: judge on the strength of the arts/culture/storytelling reporting first.
- 80-100: Excellent arts, culture, or storytelling journalism. Cariboo/Williams Lake arts news lands here (arts council grants, murals, local festivals, Indigenous film, community theatre, heritage programs, a Cariboo author or artist honoured) — and so does outstanding national or international cultural reporting with real depth.
- 55-79: Solid arts/culture/media journalism. Rural BC and Canadian cultural coverage, CBC Arts features, regional festivals, community media projects, heritage preservation, creative-economy stories, digital storytelling tools and platforms, community media tech (podcasting, streaming, local publishing), animation and film production. Most genuine cultural journalism belongs HERE, not below.
- 30-54: Mainstream entertainment-industry coverage with modest substance (awards-show results, film/TV/music business news, publishing trade news).
- 15-29: Tangentially creative — a tech feature touching media/publishing/streaming, or Cariboo civic news with no arts angle.

ANCHORS: 'Repatriated Tŝilhqot'in baskets arrive in Williams Lake from Brooklyn Museum' → 95. 'How a BC First Nation is digitizing its oral histories' → 80. 'CBC Arts: the quiet revival of small-town prairie theatre' → 68. 'Netflix reports Q3 subscriber growth' → 20.

Score 0-100 where 100 is a perfect thematic match and 0 is completely unrelated.

Linda Lou Howarth of Tatla Lake, located west of Williams Lake, couldn’t be more proud of her grandson as she continues to sell homemade breads and buns to be able to watch him compete in Las Vegas at the upcoming YETI Junior National Finals Rodeo (NFR). Tanner Loring, 16, of Riske Creek is one of more than 700 young cowboys and cowgirls who will be heading to the entertainment capital of the world in December after qualifying for novice bull riding. In Williams Lake at the Bewitching Market on Saturday, Oct. 10, Linda could be found with Tanner’s great-aunt Ivy Bowe selling fresh frybread and fry dawgs. Sales that evening went towards paying for Linda and her husband, Loring’s grandfather, flight to Vegas to watch their grandson. “When I heard he was going to Vegas, I just hit every market I could to sell bread, and I’m doing quite well,” Linda said, adding that when her grandson is on television, she’s glued to the screen. In addition to the Bewitching Market, Linda also baked bread and buns to sell at various markets throughout the area over the summer. Bella Coola was where she was most successful with her sales, supporting their travel to Las Vegas. She has raised over $2,000. “We’re quite excited,” Linda said, adding she was able to watch Tanner compete in the B.C. Rodeo Association’s (BCRA) POLARIS Championship Finals Rodeo held at the 77th North Thompson Fall Fair & Rodeo in Barriere. items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

Use of death penalty against people for crimes committed when they were children a ‘new low’, say rights groups

A young man faces imminent execution in Saudi Arabia for attending protests and funerals when he was aged 15 to 17, say human rights groups, in the latest example of the kingdom’s surging use of the death penalty for non-violent crimes.

Youssef al-Manasif was arrested in 2017 and accused of crimes including joining demonstrations for religious freedom by the Shia minority and attending funerals that the Saudi authorities deem to be protests. He was convicted and sentenced to death by the specialised criminal court, a secretive tribunal set up for terrorism-related cases.

items.title: [ArchDaily] World Monuments Watch 2027 Nominations Point to Government Austerity, Climate Impact and Skills Shortages as Main Threats to Heritage
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

The World Monuments Fund (WMF), an independent nonprofit organization dedicated to the preservation of historic architecture and cultural heritage since 1965, receives nominations through the World Monuments Watch, a flagship advocacy and conservation program. Every two years, the Watch selects 25 sites from the nominations received from individuals and community-based organizations worldwide. Nominations for the 2027 World Monuments Watch closed on March 20, 2026, with a total of 372 public nominations from 84 countries and territories. Before announcing the selected sites in early 2027, the WMF offers an analysis of the nominations. Global data shows three main causes of heritage endangerment worldwide: government austerity, intensifying climate impact, and lack of access to specialized skills and expertise. At a time when political priorities tend to stray from history, the call is to recognize heritage sites as an area of shared opportunity rather than a burden.

items.title: [japantoday.com] Carney urges Alberta voters to reject path to separation and nine other proposals
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

Prime Minister Mark Carney urged Albertans at a Calgary rally Thursday to vote to keep the province in Canada and reject nine other referendum proposals in the Oct. 19 vote [timescolonist.com#1][cbc.ca#1]. The ballot does not decide independence directly: it asks whether Alberta should remain in Canada or begin the legal process for a future binding separation referendum [oneindia.com#1][dw.com#1]. Carney warned that a vote against Canada could bring years of division and uncertainty, while acknowledging that Alberta’s grievances with Ottawa are real. He cited the proposed Pacific Link pipeline as evidence of federal support for the province. Alberta Premier Danielle Smith, who also supports remaining in Canada, argues that voters should approve the other nine questions to press Ottawa for more provincial autonomy [aa.com.tr#1][cbc.ca#1][calgaryherald.com#2]. A pro-unity rally is scheduled in Edmonton on Friday, and federal Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre is scheduled to speak in Calgary. Voters cast more than 186,000 ballots in Wednesday’s advance poll, and Elections Alberta had received and processed 454,000 special ballots, according to figures reported by the Calgary Herald [timescolonist.com#1][calgaryherald.com#1].

items.title: [downes.ca] When AI Can Make Almost Anything, Judgment Becomes the Job
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

Mike Taylor, Mike Taylor | Learning Designer, Speaker & Author, Oct 16, 2026

The argument here, stated about half way through the post, is that "when content becomes abundant, judgment becomes scarce." So "that is where learning professionals can bring more value." Let's think about that. A while ago I proposed a type of AI, called "deontic analytics", would decide what is worthwhile, what is valuable, what should be done. I've seen nothing that suggests AI will be incapable of this. Why would we trust human judgement over AI, if AI can be demonstrably better at this? Consider the new decision models, like Jev and Clef and Decision 1.0 (I'll be a human named that one). It's not obvious that human judgement will always be better. Image: Shadhin.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Scientists discover how exercise reverses muscle aging
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

Scientists have uncovered a hidden biological mechanism that helps explain how exercise can reverse some of the damage caused by muscle aging. The key is a gene called DEAF1, which becomes overactive with age and interferes with the muscles’ ability to clear damaged proteins and repair themselves. Exercise can help restore this balance, allowing older muscles to rebuild and regain strength, although the benefits may diminish when the system becomes too disrupted.

items.title: [ArchDaily] What Should Exterior Insulation Do Beyond Thermal Performance?
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

The buildings and construction sector accounts for around 39% of global CO₂ emissions and nearly 50 per cent of global material extraction. Operational carbon emissions which are associated with the energy consumed to run the buildings also rose by 1% to 9.9 billion tonnes of CO₂ in 2024, even as building energy use intensity (EUI) has improved. These figures point to persistent gaps in the way buildings are designed, constructed and upgraded. One important area for closing those gaps is the building envelope insulation, which remains central to controlling energy demand, improving thermal resilience and reducing carbon emissions.
